entries.clue: Hairline fractures finally seen in window that’s not new – tip! (6,4)

indicatorNotes.finally: finally points to the end of the word before it, so take the last letter of 'fractures'
indicatorNotes.not new: new is abbreviated N, so 'not new' strips that letter out of 'window'

blocks.note: a tip is a peak, the pointed top of something

annotation.surface: Someone spots hairline cracks in an old window and passes on a handy tip.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hairline fractures' reads as one phrase about cracked glass, but 'Hairline' stands alone as the definition. The dash and exclamation make 'tip' look like advice; it is a pointed top.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a V-shaped point of hair at the middle of the forehead is one particular hairline.

entries.clue: Aha! Somewhere to get a drink! (4)

blocks.note: an exclamation of surprise or discovery
a shaft sunk into the ground to draw water

annotation.surface: Someone thirsty cries out on spotting a place to get a drink.
annotation.walkthrough: One word does two jobs: WELL is both an exclamation and a source of water. The surface makes it one delighted moment of discovery.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses are everyday: 'Well!' as an interjection of surprise, and a well as a water source.

entries.clue: Twice act the fool (4)

indicatorNotes.Twice: twice means two times, so the next piece is written out twice

blocks.note: the same two letters a second time

annotation.surface: An instruction to play the clown not once but twice.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Act the fool' reads as one idiom, but it splits: 'act' is the wordplay and 'fool' the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: An informal sense: the extinct flightless bird lends its name to a stupid or behind-the-times person.

entries.clue: Pa, can we read novel – a big one? (3,3,5)

indicatorNotes.novel: as an adjective novel means new, so the letters are put into a new order

annotation.surface: A child asks their father whether they can tackle a novel together – a really big one.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Novel' works twice: as an adjective meaning new it rearranges the letters, and as a noun it starts the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Tolstoy's book runs to well over a thousand pages, the byword for a very long novel.

entries.clue: Forecaster making net gains in speech (7)

indicatorNotes.in speech: in speech means as spoken, so the word is heard, not seen

blocks.note: net gains are what a business keeps after costs; spoken, it matches a word for a seer

annotation.surface: A pundit whose predictions pay off when he speaks.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Making' is the link. 'Net' is not fishing gear but the sense left after deductions.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: someone who foretells what is coming.

entries.clue: Warned: treadle malfunctioning (7)

indicatorNotes.malfunctioning: a malfunctioning machine has its parts out of order, and so do these letters

annotation.surface: A notice that the foot pedal on a sewing machine has broken.
annotation.walkthrough: A treadle is a foot-operated pedal driving a machine such as an old sewing machine.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: put on guard about a danger.

entries.clue: He’s in the OT in biblical tower, scratching head (4)

indicatorNotes.scratching head: to scratch is to strike out, so the head, the first letter, goes

blocks.note: the Tower of Babel in Genesis
the first letter of that tower's name, struck out

annotation.surface: A figure from the Old Testament stands puzzled in the Tower of Babel.
annotation.walkthrough: OT is the Old Testament. 'Scratching head' looks like puzzlement, which suits Babel's confusion of tongues.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Adam and Eve's second son, killed by Cain, is one of the Old Testament's figures.

entries.clue: Small bird illegally traded? I bet (7,3)

indicatorNotes.illegally: done illegally means not by the rules, so the letters are not in their proper order

annotation.surface: Someone suspects a small bird has been sold on the black market.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark and 'I bet' read as a speaker's sceptical aside, but all those letters are fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a small tawny reed-bed bird whose male has black 'moustache' markings.

entries.clue: Sadly hit by snarl where dead ends abound (10)

annotation.definitionNote: the definition describes a kind of place; the answer is plural

indicatorNotes.Sadly: sadly can mean in a sorry state, badly done, so the letters are in a mess

annotation.surface: Someone snarled at in a place where every road seems to lead nowhere.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Snarl' also means a tangle, which fits a maze nicely, but here it is only letters.
annotation.definitionFit: By description: mazes are built of branching paths, most of them closed off.

entries.clue: Short trousers and red heels on, dancing (10)

indicatorNotes.dancing: dancers move about and swap places, and the letters do the same

annotation.surface: A dancer kitted out in shorts and red heels.
annotation.walkthrough: 'And' reads as joining two items of clothing; it only links definition to wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: By description: the leather shorts of Bavarian and Austrian folk dress.

entries.clue: Clothing to boast about (4)

indicatorNotes.about: to turn about is to turn round, so the word is read backwards

blocks.note: to boast is to brag, and those four letters are set down from the back

annotation.surface: An outfit worth showing off about.
annotation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like 'concerning' after 'boast'; it turns the boast round.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, usually for distinctive dress: clerical garb.

entries.clue: It’s almost always off the charts (3-3,6)

annotation.definition: It’s almost always off the charts

blocks.note: not quite always: there was one exception
the surface pushes 'extraordinary'; taken literally it means absent from the pop charts

annotation.surface: Something so extreme it is literally off the scale.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Off the charts' usually means extraordinary; read literally it means absent from the pop charts, where this act appeared only once.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom for an artist known for a single hit record, and so almost never in the charts.

entries.clue: Clear at the outset, Everyman’s on rugby pitch, unwell and too old (4-3-4)

indicatorNotes.at the outset: the outset is the start, so this piece comes first
indicatorNotes.on: in a down clue, one piece sits on top of the next

blocks.note: the goalposts on a rugby pitch are H-shaped

annotation.surface: The setter, out on the rugby field, admits feeling poorly and past it.
annotation.walkthrough: Everyman is also the setter's name, so the clue sounds like a self-portrait; here it just gives HE. The 's is 'is', letting HE sit on top of H in the down entry.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: past one's prime, like someone who has climbed to the top and is on the way down.

entries.clue: Bob Marley song I Shot the Sheriff’s intro, live, remastered (2,4,4)

indicatorNotes.intro: the intro of a piece is its opening, so take the first letter
indicatorNotes.remastered: a remastered track is reworked, so the letters are rearranged

annotation.surface: A live, remastered recording of the opening to Marley's I Shot the Sheriff.
annotation.walkthrough: The song title 'I Shot the Sheriff' must be broken apart: 'I Shot' is taken whole, but only the S of 'Sheriff'.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a 1978 single by Bob Marley and the Wailers.

entries.clue: In line? I nearly ran, being obstinate (10)

indicatorNotes.nearly: nearly means not quite all, so the word stops one letter short

blocks.note: a flex is British for an electric cable or cord
ran = BLED, as colours do in the wash, less its last letter

annotation.surface: Someone in a queue confesses they almost ran off, being too stubborn to wait.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ran' is not running but colours running in the wash: BLED.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: unwilling to bend or change one's mind.

entries.clue: Constituents of saliva in play area? (7)

blocks.note: saliva = spit; its first letter is one constituent
listing the parts joins them with 'and'
the rest of spit is the other constituent

annotation.surface: A question about what is in the spit found in a children's play area.
annotation.walkthrough: The wordplay runs backwards: SPIT is made of the parts S and PIT, and the phrase describing that, 'S and PIT', spells the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a sand-filled hollow where children dig and play.

entries.clue: André’s denounced, to some extent, somewhere on the Elbe … (7)

indicatorNotes.to some extent: to some extent means partly, so only part of the phrase is used

annotation.surface: André has been denounced somewhere along a German river.
annotation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs into the next clue, but each clue is solved on its own.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the capital of Saxony, in eastern Germany, straddles the River Elbe.

entries.clue: … French president losing energy in part of Benelux (7)

indicatorNotes.losing: to lose something is to be left without it, so the letter goes

annotation.surface: A former French president runs out of energy in the Low Countries.
annotation.walkthrough: Benelux is Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose sense: the name of the Netherlands' western provinces is widely used for the whole country, one of the three Benelux states.

entries.clue: Diminish empty, desolate expanse (7)

indicatorNotes.empty: emptying a word removes its insides, leaving the outer letters

blocks.note: a tract is an expanse of land

annotation.surface: A bleak, empty wasteland that shrinks away.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Empty' and 'desolate' look like two synonyms side by side; the first empties the second.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, usually followed by 'from': to lessen the worth of something.

entries.clue: He ignores issues over case of suet that’s fattening (7)

indicatorNotes.case of: a case is the outside of something, so take the outer letters

blocks.note: O = over, as in cricket scoring

annotation.surface: Someone ignoring warnings about a suet pudding's calories.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Issues over' reads as one phrase; 'over' is O. Suet is hard animal fat used in British puddings.
annotation.definitionFit: A figurative sense: the bird is said to bury its head in the sand, so a person who refuses to face problems is called one.

entries.clue: Characters from Tinseltown go along to see player’s worst fear (3,4)

indicatorNotes.Characters from: characters are letters, so take some of the letters of the words that follow

annotation.surface: Hollywood actors go along to watch a footballer's nightmare.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Characters from Tinseltown' looks like film stars and makes 'Tinseltown' seem the only source; the letters run on through 'go along'.
annotation.definitionFit: By description: putting the ball into your own net is the mistake every footballer dreads.

entries.clue: What you expect with cricket: below lifeless (3,4,5)

blocks.note: a cricket, the insect, has six legs, each with a foot

annotation.surface: A complaint that watching cricket is deathly dull.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cricket' is the insect, not the game, and the number is a count of legs rather than a hit to the boundary.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: buried in a grave, so dead.

entries.clue: Proudly impenitent artiste française, primarily! (4)

indicatorNotes.primarily: primarily means first of all, so take the first letter of each word

annotation.surface: A tribute to a French singer who was proud to regret nothing.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue also describes the answer: Édith Piaf sang 'Non, je ne regrette rien', a proud refusal to repent.
annotation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: the French chanteuse's signature song declares she regrets nothing.

entries.clue: River goddess (4)

blocks.note: the Thames takes a different name as it flows through Oxford
the Egyptian mother goddess, wife of Osiris

annotation.walkthrough: The Thames is called the Isis in Oxford, a favourite crossword river.
annotation.definitionFit: Two proper names that happen to coincide: an Oxford stretch of the Thames and an Egyptian deity.

entries.clue: Brother repulsed by small globes (4)

indicatorNotes.repulsed: repulsed means driven back, so the word is turned round

blocks.note: bro = brother, pushed back so it reads from the end

annotation.surface: A brother is disgusted by some little balls.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Repulsed' looks like disgust; it means driven back, which reverses BRO.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: spheres, like the jewelled ball a monarch holds.

entries.clue: Greatest parts of capitals etc with carbon reduction (10)

indicatorNotes.reduction: reducing something makes it smaller, here by one letter

blocks.note: capitals and the like are major cities
C = carbon, the letter taken out

annotation.surface: A study of carbon cuts in the biggest parts of capital cities.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is an environmental report; 'with carbon reduction' means take C out of MAJOR CITIES.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the larger shares of a whole, as in a vote.

blocks.note: a fifty-fifty chance, in betting terms

annotation.surface: A sum that looks like arithmetic: fifty divided by fifty, and is the result odd?
annotation.walkthrough: The slash looks like division, making 50/50 = 1, which is odd; read as a chance it is the opposite.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses are standard: an equal chance, and a whole number divisible by two.

entries.clue: Even so, sentences that depict fruit etc (5,5)

annotation.definitionNote: elliptical: read as '[pictures] that depict fruit etc'
annotation.surface: A remark about sentences that describe bowls of fruit.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sentences' are prison terms, not grammar. The painting's plural keeps the F.
annotation.definitionFit: By description: paintings of arranged objects such as fruit, flowers and jugs.
